completed_response.text:
Not every countable group is MF in the operator norm approximation sense. We prove a one-sided compression criterion that places normal property (T) subgroups in the MF radical. Normal generation can make that radical equal the whole group. An elementary group over the binary Leavitt algebra satisfies the criterion, giving a simple property (T) group that is not MF. We also prove exact pullback formulas showing that a kernel invisible to MF preserves the complete family of MF quotients above it.
Introduction
A countable group is MF if it embeds in the unitary group of a norm matrix corona 𝒬_(d) = ∏_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ)/⨁_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ). Here ⨁_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ) = {(x_(n)) ∈ ∏_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ): ∥x_(n)∥ → 0} is the c₀-direct sum. Equivalently, an MF group admits finite-dimensional unitary models whose multiplicative defects tend to zero in operator norm. These models asymptotically separate its nonidentity elements: for each g ≠ 1, the quantity limsup_(n)∥V_(n)(g) − 1∥ is positive, with a lower bound that may depend on g. This is the operator norm notion of MF group introduced by Carrión–Dadarlat–Eckhardt [citation omitted].
For a countable group G, define its MF radical by Rad_(MF)(G) = ⋂_(d)⋂_(π: G → 𝒰(𝒬_(d)))ker π. Proposition 1 shows that G is MF precisely when Rad_(MF)(G) is trivial. If Rad_(MF)(G) = G, every homomorphism from G to an MF group is trivial.
More generally, for N ⊴ G define its MF kernel closure by cl_(MF)^(G)(N) = ⋂{ker f: N ≤ ker f, f: G → M, M MF}. The image of a corona homomorphism from G is countable and is itself MF; conversely, every MF target embeds in a norm matrix corona. Thus Rad_(MF)(G) = cl_(MF)^(G)(1), and G/N is MF precisely when cl_(MF)^(G)(N) = N. This is a closure operation on the normal subgroups of one fixed group; it is unrelated to topological closure of classes of marked groups.
Proposition 1 (basic properties of the MF radical). For every countable group G, the subgroup Rad_(MF)(G) is fully invariant, the quotient G/Rad_(MF)(G) is MF, and G/N is MF ⇔ cl_(MF)^(G)(N) = N (N ⊴ G). In particular, G is MF if and only if its MF radical is trivial.
Proof. An intersection of kernels is normal. If α is an endomorphism of G, x ∈ Rad_(MF)(G), and π is a corona homomorphism of G, then π ∘ α kills x. Hence π(α(x)) = 1 for every π, which proves full invariance.
Put R = Rad_(MF)(G) and enumerate the nonidentity elements of G/R as (x_(j))_(j ≥ 1) and the pairs in (G/R)². For each x_(j), the definition of R supplies a corona homomorphism whose value at x_(j) has positive distance from the identity. Every such homomorphism kills R and therefore descends to G/R. Choose coordinate unitary lifts, using polar correction as in Lemma 7. At stage n, take a direct sum of one coordinate from each of the first n models. Choose each coordinate far enough out that the first n multiplication defects are at most 1/n and the designated value at x_(j) retains at least half of its corona norm separation. Such coordinates exist arbitrarily far out: the defects converge to zero, while the quotient norm is a limsup. The resulting operator norm asymptotic representation detects every x_(j), so its corona homomorphism is faithful on G/R. Thus G/R is MF.
Applied to G/N, the same argument says that G/N is MF exactly when the intersection of the kernels of all maps into MF groups that kill N is N, which is the asserted closure criterion. ◻
For a subgroup L ≤ G, put Comp_(G)(L) = {u ∈ G: uLu⁻¹ ≤ L} and define its compression–centralizer defect by 𝔇_(G)(L) = ⟨ ⟨[ucu⁻¹, ℓ]: u ∈ Comp_(G)(L), c ∈ C_(G)(L), ℓ ∈ L⟩ ⟩_(G).
Theorem 1 (one-sided compression criterion). Let G be countable and let L ≤ G have property (T). If K ⊴ G has property (T) and K ≤ 𝔇_(G)(L), then K ≤ Rad_(MF)(G). In particular, a nontrivial such K makes G non-MF. If G has property (T) and 𝔇_(G)(L) = G, then Rad_(MF)(G) = G.
Corollary 6 puts 𝔇_(G)(L) in the kernel detected by normalized Hilbert–Schmidt norm. If a corona representation were nontrivial on K, normality of K would make its Kazhdan projection commute with the image of G. The complementary corner would then contain no K-fixed vectors. A Kazhdan inequality gives an element of K whose Hilbert–Schmidt distance from the identity is bounded below there. This contradicts the Hilbert–Schmidt triviality of the defect elements. Independently, Theorem 2 shows that every finite-dimensional linear representation over every field kills 𝔇_(G)(L).
The question whether every countable group is MF remained open [citation omitted]. Applying Theorem 1 to the binary Leavitt construction below answers the question.
Let L_(𝔽₂)(1, 2) denote the binary Leavitt algebra. It is the unital 𝔽₂-algebra generated by s₀, s₁, t₀, t₁ subject to t_(i)s_(j) = δ_(ij), s₀t₀ + s₁t₁ = 1. For a unital ring R, write e_(ij)(a) = 1 + aE_(ij) and let EL_(n)(R) be the subgroup of GL_(n)(R) generated by the elements e_(ij)(a), i ≠ j.
Theorem 2 (the binary Leavitt group). Put R = L_(𝔽₂)(1, 2) and H = EL₁₂(R). Then H is nontrivial, simple, has property (T), and Rad_(MF)(H) = H. Equivalently, every homomorphism from H to an MF group is trivial. In particular, H is non-MF.
Inside H, an explicit element τ satisfies τLτ⁻¹ ≤ L for the subgroup L ≅ EL₃(R) in the upper left. The element c = e₃₄(1) centralizes L, and for ℓ = e₁₂(1) the corresponding commutator is d = e₀₂(s₁t₁). The relation t₁(s₁t₁)s₁ = 1 and the elementary commutator relations show directly that d normally generates H. Since d ∈ 𝔇_(H)(L) and 𝔇_(H)(L) is normal, it follows that 𝔇_(H)(L) = H. Therefore Theorem 1 gives Rad_(MF)(H) = H.
If ρ: G → GL (V) is a homomorphism and V is finite-dimensional, conjugation by ρ(u) maps the commutant of ρ(L) injectively into itself, hence bijectively. Thus ρ kills 𝔇_(G)(L). Consequently, 𝔇_(G)(L) = 1 if G has a faithful finite-dimensional linear representation. The same conclusion holds if G is residually finite, because every nonidentity element then survives in a finite permutation representation. If G is amenable, its property-(T) subgroup L is finite [citation omitted]; then uLu⁻¹ = L, so ucu⁻¹ centralizes L for every u ∈ Comp_(G)(L), and again 𝔇_(G)(L) = 1.
The argument is specific to operator norm approximation and gives no conclusion about soficity or hyperlinearity: normalized Hilbert–Schmidt approximations do not provide the operator norm control used to construct the conjugation representation in Theorem 5.
A full MF radical also lets us prescribe the quotient visible to MF.
Theorem 3 (prescribed quotients visible to MF). Let B be a countable group with Rad_(MF)(B) = B, and let 1 ≠ d ∈ B normally generate B. Put A = ⟨d⟩ and, for a countable group Q, define W_(Q) = B*_(A)(Q × A). Then the map π_(Q): W_(Q) → Q which kills B and projects the second vertex group onto Q is a split epimorphism, and Rad_(MF)(W_(Q)) = π_(Q)⁻¹(Rad_(MF)(Q)). The group W_(Q) is non-MF. If Q is MF, then Rad_(MF)(W_(Q)) = ker π_(Q) = ⟨ ⟨d⟩ ⟩_(W_(Q)). Moreover, precomposition with π_(Q) induces a bijection Hom (Q, M) → Hom (W_(Q), M) for every MF group M.
Relation to prior work
Carrión–Dadarlat–Eckhardt introduced the framework for MF groups used here [citation omitted]; Korchagin subsequently developed permanence and local approximation results for MF groups [citation omitted]. Shulman proves MF permanence for doubles G*_(H)G of MF groups. Separately, Shulman proves MF full group C^(*)-algebra results for several classes of amalgamated and semidirect products [citation omitted]. The operator norm case remained open after failure of approximation had been established for finite Schatten norms [citation omitted]. Bachner–Dogon–Lubotzky study stability between the operator and Hilbert–Schmidt norms as a possible source of non-MF groups [citation omitted]. Here operator norm control implies that coordinatewise conjugation defines a representation in a second norm matrix corona. The Kazhdan projection of this conjugation representation makes the Hilbert–Schmidt asymptotic commutant invariant under the one-sided compressor. Theorem 8 then proves that a normal property-(T) subgroup contained in the defect lies in the MF radical.
Leavitt introduced the algebras L_(K)(1, n) as examples of rings with nonunique module rank [citation omitted]. Their defining relations supply the internal compression used here. The binary Leavitt algebra is purely infinite simple [citation omitted], hence an exchange ring [citation omitted], and its center is the base field [citation omitted]. Preusser’s work gives general theorems about normal subgroups of linear groups over exchange rings [citation omitted]; the simplicity proof below instead extracts an elementary root directly from a nonidentity normal element. Ershov–Jaikin-Zapirain give property (T) for EL_(n)(R) whenever n ≥ 3 and R is a finitely generated unital associative ring [citation omitted]. Related rigidity results for metric approximations of Kazhdan groups appear in [citation omitted].
One-sided compression in finite dimension
Theorem 2 (finite-dimensional commutant rigidity). Let G be a group, let L ≤ G, and suppose u ∈ G satisfies uLu⁻¹ ≤ L. If k is a field, V is a finite-dimensional k-vector space, and ρ: G → GL (V) is a homomorphism, then ρ(u)ρ(L)^(′)ρ(u)⁻¹ = ρ(L)^(′), where ρ(L)^(′) is the commutant of ρ(L) in End_(k)(V). Consequently, if c ∈ C_(G)(L), then ρ([ucu⁻¹, ℓ]) = 1 (ℓ ∈ L).
Proof. Put C = ρ(L)^(′). If x ∈ C, h ∈ L, and h^(′) = uhu⁻¹ ∈ L, then [complex mathematical display]. Thus ρ(u)⁻¹Cρ(u) ⊆ C. Conjugation by ρ(u)⁻¹ is injective, and C is finite-dimensional. Its restriction to C is therefore surjective, so the inclusion is equality. Conjugating by ρ(u) gives ρ(u)Cρ(u)⁻¹ = C.
If c ∈ C_(G)(L), then ρ(c) ∈ C, hence ρ(ucu⁻¹) ∈ C. Therefore ρ([ucu⁻¹, ℓ]) = 1 for every ℓ ∈ L. ◻
The finite-dimensional hypothesis is essential here. On an infinite-dimensional space an injective endomorphism of the commutant need not be surjective. In Section 3 the Kazhdan projection places the analogous endomorphism inside a norm matrix corona, where stable finiteness supplies the missing surjectivity for projections onto fixed vectors.

Lemma 3. For every sequence (m_(n)), the norm matrix corona ∏_(n)M_(m_(n))(ℂ)/⨁_(n)M_(m_(n))(ℂ) is stably finite. Consequently, unitarily equivalent projections in a norm matrix corona are equal whenever one is dominated by the other.

Lemma 4 (one-sided order for the Kazhdan projection). Let L have property (T), let B be a unital C^(*)-algebra, and let π: L → 𝒰(B) be a homomorphism. Denote by P ∈ B the image of the Kazhdan projection under the extension C_(max)^(*)(L) → B. If U ∈ 𝒰(B) satisfies Uπ(L)U^(*) ⊆ π(L), then U^(*)PU ≤ P.

Hence U^(*)Fix π(L) ⊆ Fix π(L), so the range projection U^(*)PU is dominated by P in B(ℋ). Faithfulness of the representation gives the same projection inequality in B. ◻
Theorem 5 (one-sided Kazhdan transport). Let L ≤ G have property (T), and let u ∈ G satisfy uLu⁻¹ ≤ L. Let (V_(n)) be an operator norm asymptotic representation of G. Then Ad (V(u))(𝒞₂(V, L)) = 𝒞₂(V, L).
Proof. Fix x = (x_(n)) ∈ 𝒞₂(V, L) and let ω be a free ultrafilter. Regard M_(d_(n))(ℂ) as a Hilbert space with its normalized Hilbert–Schmidt inner product, and form the ultraproduct of Hilbert spaces 𝒦_(ω). Conjugation by the V_(n)(g) defines a unitary representation σ of G on 𝒦_(ω). Indeed, for unitaries A, B one has ∥Ad (A) − Ad (B)∥ ≤ 2∥A − B∥, so the operator norm multiplicative defects of (V_(n)) also make the conjugation actions multiplicative modulo c₀. Corollary 6. Let L ≤ G have property (T), let uLu⁻¹ ≤ L, and let c ∈ C_(G)(L). Then [ucu⁻¹, ℓ] ∈ R_(∞ → 2)(G) (ℓ ∈ L).
Proof. Let (V_(n)) be an operator norm asymptotic representation. If c ∈ C_(G)(L), then (V_(n)(c)) ∈ 𝒞₂(V, L). By Theorem 5, the same is true of (V_(n)(u)V_(n)(c)V_(n)(u)^(*)). Asymptotic multiplicativity identifies this sequence in operator norm with (V_(n)(ucu⁻¹)); explicitly, ∥V_(n)(u)V_(n)(c)V_(n)(u)^(*) − V_(n)(ucu⁻¹)∥ → 0. Therefore ∥V_(n)([ucu⁻¹, ℓ]) − 1∥₂ → 0 (ℓ ∈ L). Intersecting over (V_(n)) proves the claim. ◻
Normal Kazhdan subgroups and the MF radical
Let K ⊴ G have property (T), and let p be the image of its Kazhdan projection under a corona representation of G. Normality of K implies that p commutes with the image of G. Hence q = 1 − p also commutes with that image, and the corner q𝒬_(d)q has no nonzero K-fixed vectors.
Lemma 7 (central corona corners). Let ρ: G → 𝒰(𝒬_(d)) be a homomorphism from a countable group, and let q ∈ 𝒬_(d) be a nonzero projection commuting with ρ(G). Then, after passing to an infinite coordinate subsequence, there are nonzero projections q_(n) ∈ M_(d_(n))(ℂ) and an operator norm asymptotic representation W_(n): G → 𝒰(q_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ)q_(n)) whose corona class is the corner representation g ↦ qρ(g).
Proof. Lift q to projections q_(n), and lift each ρ(g) to unitaries U_(n)(g). The first lift is obtained by spectral rounding; the second is obtained by polar correction, since the two unitarity defects of any lift converge to zero in operator norm. The commutation relation in the corona gives ∥q_(n)U_(n)(g) − U_(n)(g)q_(n)∥ → 0 (g ∈ G). Consequently q_(n)U_(n)(g)q_(n), viewed on q_(n)ℂ^(d_(n)), has both unitarity defects converging to zero. Its polar correction W_(n)(g) is unitary and satisfies ∥W_(n)(g) − q_(n)U_(n)(g)q_(n)∥ → 0. The homomorphism relation for ρ now makes (W_(n)) an operator norm asymptotic representation. Since q ≠ 0, infinitely many q_(n) are nonzero; retain those coordinates. ◻
Theorem 8 (normal Kazhdan radical theorem). Let G be countable, let D ≤ R_(∞ → 2)(G), and let K ⊴ G have property (T) with K ≤ D. Then K ≤ Rad_(MF)(G).
Proof. Suppose that a homomorphism Θ: G → 𝒰(𝒬_(d)) is nontrivial on K. Replace G by Θ(G), replace K by Θ(K), and denote the resulting inclusion into the corona again by Θ. The new K is a nontrivial normal property-(T) subgroup, since property (T) passes to quotients. Every one of its elements remains in the universal Hilbert–Schmidt kernel, because any operator norm asymptotic representation of Θ(G), precomposed with the quotient map from the original group, is such a representation of the original group.
Let p_(K) ∈ C_(max)^(*)(K) be the Kazhdan projection and let p be its image in 𝒬_(d). Under any faithful representation of the corona, p is the projection onto the K-fixed vectors. Normality of K gives Θ(g)pΘ(g)^(*) = p (g ∈ G). Indeed, in a faithful representation of the corona the two projections have ranges Θ(g)Fix Θ(K) and Fix Θ(K); these agree because gKg⁻¹ = K. Put q = 1 − p. The projection q is nonzero: if p = 1, then every vector is fixed by K, so every element of K has trivial corona image. Proposition 9 (functoriality and normal generation). Let L ≤ G and put D = 𝔇_(G)(L).
If f: G → Q is a homomorphism, then f(D) ≤ 𝔇_(f(G))(f(L)). If S ≤ G is a nontrivial simple subgroup and D ∩ S ≠ 1, then S ≤ D. If in addition the normal closure of S in G is all of G, then D = G. If moreover G is countable and both L and G have property (T), then Rad_(MF)(G) = G.
Alternatively, suppose that f is onto, S ≤ D is simple, f(S) ≠ 1, and f(S) normally generates Q. Then 𝔇_(Q)(f(L)) = Q. If, in addition, G is countable and both L and G have property (T), then Rad_(MF)(Q) = Q.
Proof. If u ∈ Comp_(G)(L), then f(u)f(L)f(u)⁻¹ ≤ f(L). If c ∈ C_(G)(L), then f(c) ∈ C_(f(G))(f(L)). Therefore f takes every defining generator of D into a defining generator of 𝔇_(f(G))(f(L)). This proves the functoriality formula.
The subgroup D is normal in G, so D ∩ S is normal in S. Simplicity and D ∩ S ≠ 1 give D ∩ S = S, hence S ≤ D. Since D is normal in G, it then contains the normal closure of S. When the normal closure of S is G, this proves D = G. Under the property (T) hypotheses, Theorem 1 with K = G then gives Rad_(MF)(G) = G.
For the image statement, the functoriality formula gives f(S) ≤ 𝔇_(Q)(f(L)). The latter subgroup is normal in Q, so it contains the normal closure of f(S) and is therefore all of Q. Property (T) passes to quotients, so the final hypotheses give property (T) for both f(L) and Q. Applying Theorem 1 inside Q, with K = Q, proves the last assertion. ◻

The binary Leavitt group has full MF radical
Proposition 10. The group H = EL₁₂(R) is simple.
Proof. We use two concrete ring facts. First, for every 0 ≠ x ∈ R there are a, b ∈ R such that axb = 1. This is the form of pure infiniteness needed here [citation omitted]. Second, the only central unit of R is 1: indeed Z(R) = 𝔽₂ by [citation omitted] and 𝔽₂^(×) = {1}.
Normal generation from one root.
We first record that a nonzero root normally generates the elementary group. More generally, let S be a unital ring, let n ≥ 3, and suppose a, x, b ∈ S satisfy axb = 1. If a normal subgroup of EL_(n)(S) contains e_(ij)(x), choose k different from i and j. The elementary commutator relations give [e_(ij)(x), e_(jk)(b)] = e_(ik)(xb), [e_(ji)(a), e_(ik)(xb)] = e_(jk)(1), so the normal subgroup contains a unit root. From any e_(uv)(1) in the normal subgroup and any third index w, the relations [e_(wu)(r), e_(uv)(1)] = e_(wv)(r), [e_(uv)(1), e_(vw)(r)] = e_(uw)(r) show that the normal subgroup contains the corresponding source and target moves for every coefficient r ∈ S. Repeating these moves, using a third index when needed, gives every elementary generator. Thus, by the two-sided sandwich identity, it remains to prove that every nontrivial normal subgroup N ⊴ H contains a nonzero elementary root.
Separating two coefficients.
We also need the following coefficient-separation consequence of the Leavitt relations. Its purpose is to make one matrix product vanish while the reverse product retains a nonzero entry. If r, s ∈ R are nonzero, then there are a, b ∈ R such that arb = 0, bsar ≠ 0. For every w ∈ R there are x, y ∈ R with xwy = 0 and yx ≠ 0. This is immediate with x = y = 1 if w = 0. If yx = ds₀t₁c were zero, multiplying this equality on the left by cw and on the right by wd, and using cwd = 1, would force s₀t₁ = 0. Therefore yx ≠ 0. Carrión–Dadarlat–Eckhardt introduced the framework for MF groups used here [citation omitted]; Korchagin subsequently developed permanence and local approximation results for MF groups [citation omitted]. Separately, Shulman proves MF full group C^(*)-algebra results for several classes of amalgamated and semidirect products [citation omitted]. The operator norm case remained open after failure of approximation had been established for finite Schatten norms [citation omitted]. The binary Leavitt algebra is purely infinite simple [citation omitted], hence an exchange ring [citation omitted], and its center is the base field [citation omitted]. Not every countable group is MF in the operator norm approximation sense. We prove a one-sided compression criterion that places normal property (T) subgroups in the MF radical. Normal generation can make that radical equal the whole group. An elementary group over the binary Leavitt algebra satisfies the criterion, giving a simple property (T) group that is not MF. We also prove exact pullback formulas showing that a kernel invisible to MF preserves the complete family of MF quotients above it.

Introduction

A countable group is MF if it embeds in the unitary group of a norm matrix corona 𝒬_(d) = ∏_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ)/⨁_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ). Here ⨁_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ) = {(x_(n)) ∈ ∏_(n)M_(d_(n))(ℂ): ∥x_(n)∥ → 0} is the c₀-direct sum. Equivalently, an MF group admits finite-dimensional unitary models whose multiplicative defects tend to zero in operator norm. These models asymptotically separate its nonidentity elements: for each g ≠ 1, the quantity limsup_(n)∥V_(n)(g) − 1∥ is positive, with a lower bound that may depend on g. This is the operator norm notion of MF group introduced by Carrión–Dadarlat–Eckhardt [citation omitted].

For a countable group G, define its MF radical by Rad_(MF)(G) = ⋂_(d)⋂_(π: G → 𝒰(𝒬_(d)))ker π. Proposition 1 shows that G is MF precisely when Rad_(MF)(G) is trivial. If Rad_(MF)(G) = G, every homomorphism from G to an MF group is trivial.

More generally, for N ⊴ G define its MF kernel closure by cl_(MF)^(G)(N) = ⋂{ker f: N ≤ ker f, f: G → M, M MF}. The image of a corona homomorphism from G is countable and is itself MF; conversely, every MF target embeds in a norm matrix corona. Thus Rad_(MF)(G) = cl_(MF)^(G)(1), and G/N is MF precisely when cl_(MF)^(G)(N) = N. This is a closure operation on the normal subgroups of one fixed group; it is unrelated to topological closure of classes of marked groups.

The same factorization, restricted to homomorphisms that kill N, gives the closure formula. If this closure equals N, then it contains ker f. Thus image under f and inverse image under f give mutually inverse correspondences, preserving inclusion between the normal subgroups with MF quotient in G and in Q. Let B be a countable group with Rad_(MF)(B) = B, and let 1 ≠ d ∈ B normally generate B. Put A = ⟨d⟩. They therefore define an epimorphism π_(Q): W_(Q) → Q. It is split by the inclusion Q → Q × A → W_(Q). The normal-form theorem for amalgamated free products shows that both vertex maps in the amalgam definition are injective; in particular, d ≠ 1 in W_(Q).

Proposition 13 (universal factorization). Let T be a group such that every homomorphism B → T is trivial. Then precomposition with π_(Q) is a bijection Hom (Q, T) → Hom (W_(Q), T). Furthermore, ker π_(Q) = ⟨ ⟨d⟩ ⟩_(W_(Q)).

Proof. Let f: W_(Q) → T be a homomorphism. Its restriction to B is trivial, so its restriction to the amalgamated subgroup A is trivial. The universal property of the amalgam shows that f factors through π_(Q). The factorization is unique because π_(Q) is surjective.

The element d belongs to ker π_(Q). Conversely, quotienting W_(Q) by ⟨ ⟨d⟩ ⟩_(W_(Q)) kills B, since ⟨ ⟨d⟩ ⟩_(B) = B, and kills the A-factor of Q × A. The resulting quotient is Q, with quotient map induced by π_(Q). Hence ker π_(Q) = ⟨ ⟨d⟩ ⟩_(W_(Q)). ◻
